## Learning goals

- I will be able to load and check measurement data before graphing it.
- I will be able to create a graph with labels, units, and a useful title.
- I will be able to fit an appropriate model and explain what its parameters mean.

This is important because it enables me to turn a table of measurements into a testable relationship instead of choosing a trendline only because it looks close.

## Progression

1. Load the CSV produced in the previous lesson.
2. Check row count, column names, units, missing values, and impossible values.
3. Plot the raw points before fitting anything.
4. Begin with a linear model using a teacher dataset such as voltage versus current.
5. Plot the fitted line on the same axes.
6. Calculate residuals: measured value minus predicted value.
7. Explain the slope, intercept, fit quality, and whether the model is physically reasonable.
8. Publish the graph and interpretation on the Quarto site, then commit and push the update.

Later datasets may use polynomial or nonlinear models, but the model must come from the system and evidence, not from trying random equations.

## Evidence

Submit the code, labelled graph, model equation, residual plot or table, and a paragraph connecting the result to the original measurement problem.

## Extend your learning

- Use the [Matplotlib quick-start guide](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/quick_start.html).
- Compare a fit with and without one suspicious measurement, then justify whether that point should remain.
- Add uncertainty or repeated trials when the measurement process supports them.

## Review and reflect

What does the slope represent in your system? What can a residual plot reveal that a fitted line alone may hide?
